title: Stanley Prusiner discovered prions, infectious proteins, and won the Nobel Prize for an idea considered heretical

trailer.text: Stanley Prusiner, a physician at the University of California School of Medicine, San Francisco, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for 1997.
J. The Jewish News of Northern California wrote that he is Jewish, and Rabbi Martin Weiner said that he and his family are very committed members of the Sherith Israel synagogue.
In 1972, after one of his patients died of dementia resulting from Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, Prusiner began his work.
According to UCSF, he found no nucleic acid in the infectious agent, and many scientists considered the idea that the agent is a protein to be a heretical idea.
According to him, by the early 1990s the existence of prions was coming to be accepted in many quarters of the scientific community.

stations.title: A young physician in San Francisco

paragraphs.text: Stanley Prusiner was born on May 28, 1942 in Des Moines, and shortly afterward his father, Lawrence, was drafted into the United States Navy.
According to him, his grandfather Ben emigrated to the United States in 1896 as a young boy from Moscow.
He studied chemistry and then medicine at the University of Pennsylvania, and received his MD in 1968.
In July 1972 he began a residency in the Department of Neurology at the University of California San Francisco.
According to him, two months later he admitted a female patient who was suffering from progressive loss of memory and difficulty performing routine tasks.
According to the Nobel press release, in 1972 one of his patients died of dementia resulting from Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, and he then began his work.
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease affects about one in a million people.
According to Science, biology then held that infectious diseases were caused by organisms built from DNA or RNA, like viruses and bacteria.
According to the Nobel press release, a hypothesis arose that the infectious agent lacked nucleic acid, and it was sensational, because all infectious agents known at the time contained DNA or RNA.
According to Yale University Press, the idea that proteins cause infectious diseases contradicted the scientific understanding of the time.
According to UCSF, many scientists considered the claim that the infectious agent in rare neurological diseases is a protein to be a heretical idea.
Prusiner said that only procedures that modified proteins reduced scrapie infectivity.
According to Science, he reported that purifying scrapie-laden brain tissue down to its infectious components always left behind a protein.
According to UCSF, he looked in the prion for a nucleic acid that could direct the synthesis of new prions, and did not find one.
According to him, despite the strong convictions of many, no nucleic acid was found in the scrapie agent.
Because of the long incubation time, Prusiner used scores of mice, and in each experiment waited approximately 200 days for symptoms to appear.
According to him, the slow and expensive assays in mice restricted progress.
He says that many people cautioned him about the high risk of studies on scrapie due to the assay problems, but the warnings did not dull his enthusiasm.
According to him, he obtained modest NIH support only with considerable difficulty.
He says that the Howard Hughes Medical Institute informed him that it would not renew its support, and UCSF informed him that he would not be promoted to tenure.
According to him, the tenure decision was reversed, and he was able to continue his work.

He says that after the Howard Hughes Institute did not renew its support, he received much larger funding from the R. J. Reynolds Company, through a program administered by Fred Seitz and Maclyn McCarty, although most of his funding always came from the NIH.
According to Science, he obtained millions of dollars in grants and published his experiments widely.
According to Yale University Press, he persevered in his research despite enormous skepticism.
According to the Nobel press release, in 1982 Prusiner and his colleagues produced from diseased hamster brains a preparation that contained a single infectious agent.
According to J., that same year he announced that rare brain diseases are caused by prions.
According to J., the scientific community scoffed in disbelief.
According to the Nobel press release, the discovery was greeted with great skepticism.
According to Prusiner, virologists did not believe his hypothesis, and some investigators in the field were irate.
He says that the personal attacks of the naysayers at times became very vicious.
Rabbi Martin Weiner said that the discovery of prions was thought to be borderline crazy, and that no one believed the idea.

stations.title: The gene, the shape and the mice

paragraphs.text: In 1985 the gene that generates the prion protein was cloned, and researchers were surprised to discover that the healthy prion protein, PrP, is naturally abundant in the brain tissue of healthy people.
Prusiner collaborated with Charles Weissmann on cloning the gene.
According to the Nobel website, he identified the gene and determined that it is also present in healthy people and animals.
According to UCSF, the normal form of PrP is folded into a twisted corkscrew or helical shape, and the disease-associated form is a flattened sheet.
In 1986 Prusiner and his colleagues found that the tempo of scrapie in animals is controlled by the sequence of the PrP gene.
They produced genetically engineered mice harboring PrP genes with the human disease mutation.
Proof that the mutations cause disease was obtained when the mutant genes were introduced into the germline of mice.
Mice from which the prion gene had been removed were found to be completely resistant to infection with disease-causing prion protein.
According to UCSF, Prusiner's ideas explained how prion diseases in humans can arise spontaneously, through inheritance or through infection.
According to J., he discovered that the proteins can cause both infectious diseases and hereditary illnesses.
According to J., Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is more common among Jews of Libyan or Tunisian descent.
Most cases are not hereditary, but the sources give different rates.
The mad cow epidemic in England first became evident in 1985 and peaked in 1992.
It was transmitted to cows through feedstuff supplemented with offals from scrapie-infected sheep.

According to the source, a new variant of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease may have resulted from transmission of BSE, and since 1995 about 20 patients have been identified with symptoms resembling the disease.
Kuru in New Guinea was transmitted in connection with cannibalistic rituals.
According to the Nobel press release, all known prion diseases lead to the death of those affected.
According to the same press release, it may be possible to develop drugs that prevent the conversion of normal prion proteins to the disease-causing form.
In 1996 Prusiner guessed that within five to six years it would be possible to rationally design a drug for the disease, but added that he might be too optimistic and that it could take a decade.
According to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), about 85% of reported cases of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease are sporadic.
According to him, as prions gained wider acceptance among scientists, he received many scientific prizes.
Among them the Lasker Award, the Potamkin Prize and the Wolf Prize.
In 1996 he was among nine scientists and artists awarded the Wolf Prizes.
J. described him as a UCSF researcher who linked mad cow disease in Britain to a human brain disorder, and wrote that the prize was $100,000.
Prof. Oded Abramsky of Hadassah nominated him for the Wolf Prize and for the Nobel Prize.
Prusiner said that his first honorary degree was from the Hebrew University in Jerusalem, in 1995.
He said that he would continue to collaborate on research with the Hebrew University.
On October 6, 1997 the Nobel Assembly at the Karolinska Institute announced that he had been awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
According to UCSF, he was then 55, and the prize was awarded to him for discovering and characterizing an entirely new class of proteins, the prions.
According to Nature, scientists across the world greeted the award with delight.
According to Science, he delivered his Nobel lecture on December 8, shortly before accepting the prize in Stockholm.
According to UCSF, Prusiner credits his success to the years of hard work by his talented colleagues.
Rabbi Martin Weiner said that Prusiner and his family have been very committed members of the Sherith Israel synagogue for more than a dozen years.
According to Science News, even as Prusiner was accepting the Nobel Prize in 1997, there were still skeptics.
According to Science, Laura Manuelidis regards the protein as a pathological reaction to infection, and believes that viruses cause mad cow disease.
Days after the award was announced, Manuelidis shared her blunt assessment with The New York Times.
According to Science, Manuelidis and others say that prion experiments are easily contaminated.
According to one researcher, nucleic acids such as viral DNA or RNA may have tainted the preparations in earlier animal experiments.
According to Science, even supporters of the prion hypothesis acknowledge that misfolded PrP is sometimes found in noninfectious tissue, and not found in infectious tissue.
On July 30, 2004 Science published a study showing that purified prions cause disease when injected into the brains of genetically engineered mice.
The animals that received synthetic prions showed signs of brain damage after 380 to 660 days, and those that received saline did not.
According to Science, in PMCA experiments mice are injected with a concentrated product of brain homogenate, and because the mice get sick, many believe that prions are the infectious agent.

According to Science, Prusiner declared in his Nobel lecture on December 8 of that year, shortly before accepting the prize in Stockholm, that many attempts to disprove the prion hypothesis over the past 15 years had failed.

claims.text: לפי J. מ-1996, כ-75 אחוז ממקרי קרויצפלד-יעקב מפוזרים בין אוכלוסיות שונות.
claims.quote: But about 75 percent of CJD cases are scattered among different populations.

claims.text: מגפת הפרה המשוגעת באנגליה התבררה לראשונה ב-1985 והגיעה לשיאה ב-1992.
claims.quote: The BSE epidemic first became evident in 1985. Due to the long incubation time the epidemic did not peak until 1992.

claims.text: באנגליה הועברה מחלת הפרה המשוגעת לפרות דרך מספוא שהועשר בפסולת מכבשים שנדבקו בסקרפי.

claims.text: לפי UCSF, מחלת הקורו התפשטה בקרב אבוריג'ינים בגינאה החדשה באמצעות קניבליזם פולחני.
claims.quote: The most exotic infectious prion disease of humans is kuru, which was spread among New Guinea aborigines by ritualistic cannibalism.

claims.text: לפי הודעת הנובל, כל מחלות הפריון הידועות מובילות למוות של החולים.

claims.text: פרוזינר זכה בפרסים רבים, ביניהם פרס לסקר, פרס פוטמקין ופרס וולף.

claims.text: חוקר מ-UCSF שקשר בין מחלת הפרה המשוגעת בבריטניה להפרעת מוח אנושית זכה בפרס וולף בסך 100,000 דולר.
claims.quote: A U.C. San Francisco medical researcher who linked the mad-cow disease in Britain to a human brain disorder has been awarded the $100,000 Wolf Prize.

claims.text: פרופ' עודד אברמסקי מהדסה מועמד את פרוזינר לפרס וולף ולפרס נובל.

claims.text: לפי סיינס, מנואלידיס ואחרים טוענים שניסויי פריונים מזדהמים בקלות.
